units.title: Domain A: Nature of Science in Chemistry

outcomes.text: Say what chemistry is: the study of matter, its properties, makeup and how it interacts with energy.
Give examples showing chemistry has many sub-fields and links to other sciences.
Compare the branches of chemistry by focus, giving two everyday examples of each.
Define matter.
Tell solids, liquids and gases apart by density, compressibility and fluidity.
Recognise states of matter beyond the usual three, such as plasma and liquid crystals.
Explain the allotropes of carbon: diamond, graphite and fullerenes.
Explain how elements, compounds and mixtures differ.
Identify solutions, colloids and suspensions as mixtures and distinguish them with an example each.
Explain how temperature affects solubility and how saturated and unsaturated solutions form.
Describe an atom as a central nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons.
State that electron shells are discrete energy levels, higher ones having more energy and lying farther out.
Explain that the nucleus is held together by the strong nuclear force.
State the relative charge and mass of the electron, proton and neutron.
Link subatomic particles to their mass and charge.
Sketch how charged particles move in a uniform electric field.
Define proton (atomic) number as the number of protons in the nucleus.
Explain that proton number is unique to each element and orders the periodic table.
State that radioactive decay can change the proton number and so the element.
Define nucleon (mass) number.
Define isotopes.
State that isotopes change atomic mass but not chemical properties much.
Work out protons and neutrons in isotopes from atomic and mass numbers.
Define relative atomic mass against one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.
State that some isotopes are radioactive.
Discuss uses of isotopes such as carbon-14 dating and technetium-99 imaging.
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotope masses and abundances.
Describe how atoms form cations and anions.
Write atoms and ions with atomic number, mass number and charge notation.
Write electronic configurations of elements and ions up to proton number 20.

subtopics.title: Octet rule and types of bond

outcomes.text: Use noble gas configurations and the octet and duplet rules to predict stability.
Compare cation and anion formation by electron loss and gain.
Explain why metals are electropositive and nonmetals electronegative.
Define ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds.
Differentiate ionic and covalent compounds by bonding, structure and properties.
Explain physical properties of compounds from their bonding and structure.
Compare materials' strength and conductivity by bond type; know bonds beat intermolecular forces.
Interpret how intermolecular and electrostatic forces affect melting and boiling points.
Explain which free charged particles allow conduction in ionic, covalent and metallic substances.
Recognise that some substances ionise in water and conduct electricity.
Justify industrial uses of graphite, diamond and metals from their structure.
Draw dot-and-cross and Lewis structures for common ionic and covalent compounds.
Write chemical formulae of common elements and compounds.
Define molecular formula as the number and type of atoms in a molecule.
Define empirical formula as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
Deduce formulae and names of binary ionic compounds from ion charges.
Deduce a molecular formula from a given molecular structure.
Define the mole as the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles.
Use n = m/M and n = N/NA to find moles, mass and particle numbers.
Explain how the mole relates to Avogadro's constant.
Write balanced equations with state symbols.
Write balanced ionic equations with state symbols for reactions in solution.
Write balanced symbol equations from a written description of a reaction.
Explain a chemical system and its surroundings and how energy moves between them.
Tell exothermic from endothermic reactions with examples.
State that heat at constant pressure is enthalpy change, negative if exothermic and positive if endothermic.
Define activation energy as the minimum energy for an effective collision.
Explain that catalysts or enzymes change the pathway and so the activation energy.
Draw and label reaction pathway diagrams, with and without a catalyst.
Recognise that bond breaking takes in energy and bond making releases it.
Explain enthalpy change as energy absorbed breaking bonds minus energy released making bonds.
Calculate a reaction's enthalpy change from bond energy data.
Recognise that reversible reactions use the symbol for reversibility and may not go to completion.
Describe how changing conditions redirects a reversible reaction, e.g. hydrated copper(II) sulfate.
State that a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium in a closed system when forward and backward rates are equal.
Define Bronsted-Lowry acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
Recognise that acids give H+ ions and alkalis give OH- ions in water.
Define strong and weak acids and bases by complete or partial dissociation, with examples.
Write dissociation equations for acids and bases in water.
Recognise bases as metal oxides or hydroxides and alkalis as soluble bases.

subtopics.title: Properties of acids and bases, acid rain

outcomes.text: Describe how acids react with metals, bases and carbonates.
Identify how bases react with acids and ammonium salts.
Define acid rain.
Discuss acid rain's effects and link them to acid properties.
Define the periodic table as elements in periods and groups by increasing proton number.
Find an element's group, period or block from its electronic configuration.
Link group number to the charge of the ions an element forms.
Explain similar chemistry within a group through electronic configuration.
Identify trends across groups and periods in radius, electron affinity, electronegativity, ionisation energy, metallic character, reactivity and density.
Use names such as alkali metals, halogens, noble gases and transition metals.
Predict an element's properties from its group.
Predict an unknown element's place in the table from its electronic configuration.
Describe alkali metals as soft metals with trends down the group.
Predict properties of other group 1 elements from given information.
Order group 1 elements by reactivity from given information.
Describe halogens as diatomic non-metals with trends in density and reactivity.
Identify the appearance of the halogens at room temperature.
Explain halogen displacement reactions and halogens as oxidising agents.
Predict properties of group 17 elements from given information.
Explain the thermal stability of hydrogen halides through bond strength.
Describe transition elements: dense, high melting, variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, catalysts.
Describe noble gases as unreactive monatomic gases.
Explain noble gas unreactivity through electronic configuration.
Compare physical properties of metals and non-metals.
Describe organic molecules as straight-chain, branched or cyclic.
State that a structural formula shows unambiguously how atoms are arranged.
Identify and draw structural formulae for molecules.
State that a saturated compound has only single carbon-carbon bonds.
State that an unsaturated compound has one or more non-single carbon-carbon bonds.
Describe the general formula of compounds in a homologous series.
Identify a functional group as the atoms that fix a series' chemical properties.
Describe the general characteristics of a homologous series.
Define structural isomers, with C4H10 and C4H8 examples.
State that alkanes have single covalent bonds and are saturated.
Describe alkane combustion and chlorine substitution as a photochemical reaction.
Write equations for preparing alkanes by cracking, hydrogenation and reduction of halides.

units.title: Domain G: Activities, Lab Skills, and Practical Modules

outcomes.text: Identify apparatus from diagrams or descriptions.
Draw, complete or label diagrams of apparatus.
Explain the use of common techniques, apparatus and materials.
Choose the most appropriate apparatus or method and justify it.
Identify apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume.
Justify cm3, g and s as practical units for small amounts.
Separate a mixture by sublimation.
Explain separation methods: solvent, filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation.
Suggest separation techniques for given substances and their daily-life use.
Carry out separation and purification techniques including chromatography and electrolysis.
Describe paper chromatography to separate soluble mixtures.
Describe locating agents for colourless substances.
Interpret simple chromatograms.
State and use the equation for Rf.
Calculate concentration of an acid or base from titration data.
Assess purity from melting and boiling point information.
Describe gas tests for ammonia, CO2, chlorine, hydrogen, oxygen and SO2.
Explain flame tests for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, copper and barium.
Test for water with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
Explain testing water purity by melting and boiling point.
Distinguish distilled water from tap water.
Suggest the best apparatus or technique and justify the choice.
Describe experimental procedures.
Take readings from apparatus with suitable precision.
Take sufficient observations, repeating where appropriate.
Record qualitative observations from tests.
Record observations and measurements systematically in a table.
Record experiment results in a table.
Process data, including calculations for graph plotting.
Present data graphically with best-fit lines.
Analyse and interpret observations and graph data.
Evaluate data quality and identify anomalous results.
Identify possible sources of error in an experimental design.
State the kinetic theory assumptions and explain phase changes through particle behaviour and energy.
Distinguish evaporation from boiling.
Read heating and cooling curves using kinetic theory.
Explain qualitatively how external pressure changes boiling and evaporation.
State Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws.
Explain gas diffusion using kinetic particle theory.
Explain how molecular mass and temperature affect the rate of diffusion.
Use kinetic theory to explain why diffusion rates matter for medicines in the body.
Use the molar gas volume of 24 dm3 at r.t.p. to find gas volumes and moles.
Define concentration as solute per unit volume in g/dm3 or mol/dm3.
Calculate concentration and convert between g/dm3 and mol/dm3.
Calculate reacting masses, gas volumes and solution quantities from balanced equations.
Find empirical and molecular formulae from percentage composition.
Calculate percentage yield, percentage composition and percentage purity.
Define redox in terms of oxygen, hydrogen, electrons and oxidation state changes.
Assign oxidation numbers and use Roman numerals in names of variable-valency metals.
Identify oxidising and reducing agents in a reaction.
State that uncombined elements have oxidation number zero.
Deduce ionic formulae by balancing ion charges.
State that a monatomic ion's oxidation number equals its charge.
Explain that oxidation numbers in a neutral compound sum to zero.
Explain that oxidation numbers in an ion sum to its charge.
Test for oxidising or reducing agents using acidified permanganate or iodide colour changes.
Define electrolysis as breaking down an ionic compound with electric current.
Label the parts of a simple electrolytic cell and show electron and ion movement.
Describe electron flow, ion movement and electrode transfers during electrolysis.
Predict products and observations for electrolysis of molten PbCl2, brine and dilute sulfuric acid.
Describe products and observations in electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate.
Write half-ionic equations for electrode reactions.
Describe electroplating and its uses.

subtopics.title: Fuel cells, voltaic cells and corrosion

outcomes.text: State that a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell makes electricity with water as the only product.
Compare hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells with petrol engines.
Define corrosion and describe barrier and sacrificial protection.
Sketch a schematic diagram of a voltaic cell such as the Daniell cell.
Explain salts as ionic compounds of ions from bases and acids.
Explain why salts are solids with high melting points at STP.
Describe ionic compounds as usually solid lattice structures.
Explain why molten and dissolved salts conduct, using mobile ions.
Describe solubility trends of common salts in water.
Describe preparing, separating and purifying soluble salts from acids with alkali, metal, insoluble base or carbonate.
Describe metal reactions with dilute acids, cold water, steam and oxygen.
Order metals by reactivity from given information.
Describe the catalytic role of NO and NO2 in oxidising SO2 to SO3 in the air.
State the equation for ammonia in the Haber process.
State the sources of hydrogen and nitrogen in the Haber process.
State the Haber process conditions: 450 C, 200 atm, iron catalyst.
State the equation for SO2 to SO3 in the Contact process.
State the sources of sulfur dioxide and oxygen in the Contact process.
State the Contact process conditions and vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
Describe amphoteric oxides as reacting with both acids and bases.
Classify oxides as acidic, basic or amphoteric, including Al2O3 and ZnO.
State the composition of clean dry air: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, rest noble gases and CO2.
State the main sources of air pollutants.
State the harmful effects of CO2, CO, particulates, methane, nitrogen oxides and SO2.
Explain how CO2 and methane cause global warming.
Describe sulfur's role in acid rain and its impact.
Describe strategies against climate change and acid rain.
Describe the role of NO and NO2 in forming acid rain.
Explain how nitrogen oxides form in car engines and are removed by catalytic converters.
State that natural water may contain useful and harmful substances.
Recognise that some natural substances in water are beneficial.
Recognise that some natural substances in water are harmful.
Explain domestic water treatment: sedimentation, filtration, carbon, chlorination.
Identify negative effects of water pollutants and ways to avoid them.
Explain water scarcity in Pakistan and ways to resolve it.
State that urea, ammonium salts and nitrates are used as fertilizers.
Explain how NPK fertilizers supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Name and draw unbranched alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.
State the compound type from the name ending (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid).
Name and draw unbranched esters made from short alcohols and acids.
State that alkenes have a carbon-carbon double bond and are unsaturated.
Describe making alkenes by cracking large alkanes with heat and a catalyst.
Describe the reasons for cracking large alkanes.
Describe the test for unsaturation with aqueous bromine and KMnO4.
Describe alkene addition reactions with bromine, hydrogen and steam, and draw the products.
Write equations for making alkenes by elimination from halogenoalkanes and alcohols.
Identify alkynes as unsaturated hydrocarbons with a carbon-carbon triple bond.
Describe uses of ethyne: welding fuel and ripening fruit.

Name the uses of petroleum fractions from refinery gas to bitumen.
Describe making ethanol by fermentation and catalytic hydration, comparing both methods.
Describe the combustion of alcohols.
Discuss alcohols as fuels with advantages and disadvantages against fossil fuels.
Explain alcohols' role in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and fuel industries.
Discuss alcohols in daily life, as solvents and disinfectants.

subtopics.title: Reactions and uses of carboxylic acids

outcomes.text: Describe reactions of carboxylic acids with metals, bases and carbonates.
Describe forming ethanoic acid by oxidising ethanol, including vinegar.
Describe forming an ester from an acid and an alcohol.
Describe industrial uses of carboxylic acids and esters.
Explain the role of carboxylic acids and esters in daily life.
Define polymers as large molecules built from monomers.
Identify repeating units and linkages in addition polymers.
Deduce the repeat unit of an addition polymer from its alkene and the reverse.
State that plastics are made from polymers.

Describe environmental challenges of plastics: landfill, oceans, toxic gases from burning.
Describe proteins as natural polyamides built from amino acids.
Draw the general structure of proteins.
Draw the structure of lipids and carbohydrates.
Describe protons, neutrons and electrons by relative charge and mass.
Describe how beams of protons, neutrons and electrons deflect in an electric field.
Find the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions.

Define shell, subshell, orbital, principal quantum number and ground state.
Relate quantum numbers to how electrons are arranged in atoms.

Describe the shapes and orientations of s, p and d orbitals.
Write electronic configurations of elements and ions in shell and subshell notation.

Explain the energy order and filling order of s, p, d and f subshells.

Explain hybridisation and its types in covalent bonding.

Explain the main features of molecular orbital theory.

Recognise expanded octets in polyatomic ions such as sulfate and nitrate.
Explain dative bond formation in CO, ozone and the hydronium ion.
Interpret a balanced equation in moles, masses and gas volumes at STP.
Identify the limiting reagent by comparing mole ratios.
Find the maximum product and leftover excess reagent.
Calculate percentage yield from actual and theoretical yield.

Use molar volume at STP to find gas volume and moles.
Calculate gram molecular mass of gases from measurements at STP.
Convert between moles, mass, STP volume and particle number.
Solve multi-step stoichiometry problems using limiting reagent and yield data.
Describe London forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonding.
Describe hydrogen bonding in N-H, O-H and H-F molecules.
Use hydrogen bonding to explain water's anomalies, such as ice floating.
Explain the strength and applications of dipole forces, hydrogen bonds and London forces.
Describe evaporation, vapour pressure, boiling point, viscosity and surface tension.
Explain water's properties using hydrogen bonding.
Define molar heat of fusion and of vaporisation.
Relate heats of fusion and vaporisation to particle arrangement and energy in phase changes.
State the kinetic molecular theory assumptions for gases.
State Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws and read them graphically.
Use PV = nRT in calculations including density and Mr.
Differentiate amorphous from crystalline solids by structure and properties.
Describe crystalline solid properties: shape, melting point and cleavage planes.
Describe reactions as exothermic or endothermic by the sign of the enthalpy change.
Interpret reaction pathway diagrams showing enthalpy change and activation energy.
Define standard conditions and the enthalpies of reaction, formation, combustion and neutralisation.
Explain from bond breaking and making whether a reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
Calculate enthalpy change of reaction from bond energies.
Describe how some bond energies are exact and others are averages.
Calculate enthalpy changes from experiments using q = mc deltaT.

Do calculations with Born-Haber cycles.
Explain how ionic charge and radius affect lattice energy.
Apply enthalpy of hydration and enthalpy of solution.
Build an energy cycle linking enthalpy of solution, lattice energy and hydration.
Do calculations with energy cycles.
Explain how ionic charge and radius affect enthalpy of hydration.

Explain the sign of entropy change in state changes, heating and gas-count changes.
Calculate a reaction's entropy change from standard entropies.
Explain heat as a form of energy transfer.
Explain standard conditions and standard states for energy changes.

Apply Hess's law to multi-step reactions.
Define Gibbs free energy.
Use delta G = delta H - T delta S in problems.

subtopics.title: Rate of reaction and activation energy

Calculate with Ksp and a common ion's concentration.

Calculate the partition coefficient for a solute in two immiscible solvents.
Explain how solute and solvent polarity affect the partition coefficient.
